I have gathered substantial material from the approved sites. Here are the verse-by-verse notes.

---

## Ezekiel 30 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Structure and Date

The chapter contains two distinct prophecies: **vv. 1–19** (undated) and **vv. 20–26** (dated to the eleventh year, first month, seventh day). The second oracle comes in regular chronological order between Ezekiel 29:1–16 and chapter 31. The first oracle’s date is debated—some connect it to the same period as 29:1–16 (tenth year), others to 29:17–21 (twenty-seventh year). Ellicott judges that “there are no sufficient data for a positive determination,” but the general presumption is that an undated prophecy belongs between the dates that precede and follow it. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-30.html)

The prophecy divides into four sections marked by “Thus saith the Lord” (vv. 2, 6, 10, 13). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html)

---

### v. 1 — “Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying…”

The introductory formula marks a fresh oracle. Gill notes it is uncertain whether this prophecy was delivered around the tenth year (as the earlier part of ch. 29) or the twenty-seventh year, though he inclines toward the latter because the fulfilment is said to be “near” in v. 3. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/30.htm)

---

### v. 2 — “Son of man, prophesy and declare … Wail, ‘Alas for that day!’”

Ezekiel is told to cry out in lamentation. The words echo Isaiah 13:6 and Joel 1:11, 13. The Pulpit Commentary notes that the familiar English phrase “Woe worth the day!” is a survival of the Anglo-Saxon verb *weorthan* (German *werden*), “to become,” so its exact meaning is “Woe be to the day.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html)

Gill adds: “howl ye, ye Egyptians, and also ye Ethiopians, and all others … O the unhappy day! what a sad dismal day is this!” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/30.htm)

---

### v. 3 — “For the day is near, the Day of the LORD is near. It will be a day of clouds, a time of doom for the nations.”

**“Day of the LORD”**: The Pulpit Commentary explains that the phrase stands for any time in which Divine judgments manifest themselves in history; here it is “a time in which the heathen who had exulted in the punishment of Israel should know that the Lord was their Judge also.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html)

Ellicott says: “The judgment upon Egypt is but an individual instance, and is symbolic of general judgment upon all merely worldly power. Her fall is one step in the general overthrow of whatever exalts and opposes itself to God.” He cross-references Isaiah 13:6, 9; Joel 1:13, 15; 2:2; Obadiah 15; Zephaniah 1:7, 14. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-30.html)

**“Day of clouds”**: Keil & Delitzsch interpret this as “a day of great calamity (as in Joel 2:2).” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html) Gill notes it is a figurative use: Egypt rarely had literal rain (watered by the Nile), but now “the clouds would gather thick and black” with divine wrath. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/30.htm) David Guzik (Enduring Word) adds Wiersbe’s remark: “The Jews were led out of Egypt by a bright cloud (Exodus 13:21), but the Egyptians who once enslaved them will be under a dark cloud.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/)

**“Time of doom for the nations”** (KJV “time of the heathen”): Keil & Delitzsch say this is “a time … when heathen are judged, when their might is to be shattered (cf. Isaiah 13:22).” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html) The Pulpit Commentary agrees: the heathen who had exulted over Israel would learn that the Lord was their Judge also. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html)

**“The day is near”**: Guzik notes, “The human heart is ever prone to put off the judgment of God, easily finding solace in the unfounded thought that if God’s visitation be postponed long enough, it may never occur at all” (quoting Feinberg). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/)

---

### v. 4 — “A sword will come against Egypt … anguish in Cush … its wealth is taken away, and its foundations are torn down.”

The “sword” is the sword of the Chaldeans, coming with a commission from the Lord. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/30.htm) Cush (Ethiopia) would feel anguish (lit. “writhe convulsively,” Keil) when news reached them, fearing they would be next.

**“Foundations”**: The Pulpit Commentary takes this figuratively — “the bases of the prosperity of Egypt, its allies and mercenaries, rather than actual buildings” (cf. Psalm 11:3; 82:5). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html) Keil & Delitzsch agree: “the real foundations of the state, the regulations and institutions on which the stability and prosperity of the kingdom rest.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html) Gill allows both literal and figurative readings: foundations of cities and towers, or “her king, princes, magistrates, laws, and government.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/30.htm)

Guzik notes the audacity: “Imagine an exile from Judah, a third-rate Palestinian state … asserting that Judah’s national deity is about to bring an end to Egypt! … It was either outrageous delusion or great faith.” (quoting Vawter and Hoppe). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/)

---

### v. 5 — “Cush, Put, and Lud, and all the various peoples, as well as Libya and the men of the covenant land, will fall with Egypt by the sword.”

**Cush, Put, Lud**: Gill identifies these as sons of Ham (Cush and Phut) and Lud as son of Mizraim. They are Ethiopia, Libya, and Lydia — allies and confederates of Egypt (cf. Jeremiah 46:9). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/30.htm)

**“All the various peoples”** (KJV “all the mingled people”): Keil & Delitzsch understand this as the mercenary soldiers in the Egyptian army obtained from various nations (Greeks, Ionians, Carians). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html) Guzik agrees: “foreigners who served in the Egyptian army as mercenary soldiers” (quoting Feinberg). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/)

**“Chub” (Libya in BSB?)**: The Pulpit Commentary notes this name appears here only in Scripture and has generated many conjectures — Kufa (a district of Media), Kobe (Ethiopian coast), Cob (Mauretania), or Nubia. Keil suggests it may be a misspelling for *Lub* (Libya). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html)

**“Men of the covenant land”**: This is debated. Jerome and the LXX understood it as Judeans (Jews who fled to Egypt after Jerusalem’s fall). Hitzig and Kliefoth take it as Canaan, “the land in covenant with Jehovah.” Others argue for an unknown allied people near Egypt. Keil & Delitzsch favour an unknown but definite region. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html)

---

### v. 6 — “The allies of Egypt will fall, and her proud strength will collapse. From Migdol to Syene they will fall by the sword.”

**“They that uphold Egypt”**: The Pulpit Commentary says this includes the named allies plus the rulers, generals, perhaps even the idols of Egypt itself. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html) Keil clarifies: “Those who support Egypt” are “not the auxiliary tribes and allies … but the idols and princes (v. 13), the fortified cities (v. 15), and the warriors (v. 17), who formed the foundation of the might of the kingdom.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html)

**“From Migdol to Syene”**: From Egypt’s northern frontier to its southern border — a comprehensive sweep of the whole land. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/30.htm)

---

### v. 7 — “They will be desolate among desolate lands, and their cities will lie among ruined cities.”

Keil notes this is “almost a literal repetition of Ezekiel 29:12.” Egypt would share the fate of other lands already devastated (like Judah). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html) Gill notes that Egypt’s cities were extraordinarily numerous — Herodotus records 20,000 cities under Amasis, and other ancient sources claim 30,000 or more — and all would be ruined. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/30.htm)

---

### v. 8 — “Then they will know that I am the LORD when I set fire to Egypt and all her helpers are shattered.”

**“Set a fire”**: This is war — “War is fitly compared to fire; it feeds upon the people” (Trapp, cited in Guzik). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/) Gill renders it: “when I shall give (or set) people that are strong as fire against Egypt” (following the Targum). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/30.htm)

**“Then they will know that I am the LORD”**: This recognition formula appears repeatedly in Ezekiel. The Egyptians would learn through judgment that Yahweh — not their idols — is the true God. Guzik quotes Wiersbe: “During Israel’s sojourn in Egypt, Pharaoh wouldn’t recognize the Lord; but now the nation would learn that the Lord God of the Hebrews was indeed the only true and living God.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/)

---

### v. 9 — “On that day messengers will go out from Me in ships to frighten Cush out of complacency.”

The Pulpit Commentary notes this echoes Isaiah 18:2. The ships carry tidings of Lower Egypt’s conquest up the Nile. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html)

**Who are the messengers?** Keil argues they are not Chaldean forces but fleeing Egyptians who go by ship to Ethiopia — messengers going “from before Jehovah, who is regarded as being present in Egypt, while executing judgment there (cf. Isaiah 19:1).” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html) Clarke (cited in Guzik) says: “Ships can ascend the Nile up to Syene or Essuan, by the cataracts; and when Nebuchadnezzar’s vessels went up, they struck terror into the Ethiopians. They are represented here as the ‘messengers of God.’” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/)

**“Cush out of complacency”** (KJV “careless Ethiopians”): The Ethiopians thought themselves safe because of their remoteness. The Pulpit Commentary: “They thought themselves safe, and were lulled into a false security (comp. Isaiah 32:9–11 and Zephaniah 2:15).” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html)

**“As on the day of Egypt”**: Keil interprets this not as the present day of punishment but the ancient, well-known day of judgment upon Egypt (the Exodus plagues, Exodus 15:12). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html)

**“For it is indeed coming”**: The certainty of judgment is emphasised. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/)

---

### v. 10 — “I will put an end to the hordes of Egypt by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon.”

This is the first explicit naming of the human agent. The Pulpit Commentary notes: “Hitherto the predictions have been general. Now Ezekiel … specifies the Chaldean king.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html)

**“Hordes” (KJV “multitude”)**: Keil says the Hebrew *hamon* signifies “the tumult of the people in the possession and enjoyment of their property (cf. Ezekiel 26:13),” embracing both people and possessions — thus explained in vv. 11–12. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html)

---

### v. 11 — “He and his people with him, the most ruthless of the nations … fill the land with the slain.”

The Babylonians are described as “the most terrible of the nations” — a phrase that “struck terror in the heart of anyone” (Block, cited in Guzik). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/) Gill adds that Nebuchadnezzar’s army included troops from many conquered nations, all of them terrible. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/30.htm)

---

### v. 12 — “I will make the streams dry up and sell the land to the wicked. By the hands of foreigners I will bring desolation … I, the LORD, have spoken.”

**“Make the rivers dry”**: The Pulpit Commentary says the rivers are the Nile-branches of the Delta; their drying up points literally to a failure of the Nile inundation on which Egypt’s fertility depended, and figuratively to the failure of all sources of prosperity. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html) Keil agrees: “the arms and canals of the Nile, by which the land was watered, and on which the fertility and prosperity of Egypt depended.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html) Gill notes that drying the rivers also made the way easy and passable for the enemy. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/30.htm)

**“Sell the land into the hand of the wicked”**: To “sell” means to deliver into the power of another (cf. Deuteronomy 32:30; Judges 2:14). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html) Gill extends this to the successive foreign dominations of Egypt: Babylonians, Persians, Greeks, Romans, Saracens, Mamluks, and Turks — “all very wicked people.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/30.htm)

**“I, the LORD, have spoken”**: Guzik quotes Taylor: “Behind the hand of foreigners, who appear to act as his agents, is the word of God … which is the all-powerful ultimate agent which can turn spoken prophecy into actual fact.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/)

---

### v. 13 — “I will destroy the idols and put an end to the images in Memphis. There will no longer be a prince in Egypt, and I will instill fear in that land.”

**Memphis (Noph)**: The ancient capital of Lower Egypt, the chief centre of the worship of Ptah (whom the Greeks identified with Hephaestos). Hence the special mention of idols and images here. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html)

**“No longer a prince in Egypt”**: This means no native prince ruling over all Egypt. Gill notes that after Nectanebus was driven out by Ochus king of Persia, Egypt never again had its own king; it passed under Babylonians, Persians, Greeks, Romans, Saracens, Mamluks, and Turks. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/30.htm)

**“I will put fear in the land”**: Guzik quotes Block: “When Yahweh begins to work in Egypt, there will be fear in the land, not the reverence of devotees toward their deities or kings, but terror before Yahweh himself.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/)

---

### v. 14 — “I will lay waste Pathros, set fire to Zoan, and execute judgment on Thebes.”

**Pathros**: Upper Egypt (see note on Ezekiel 29:14). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html)

**Zoan**: The Tanis of the Greeks, an ancient city of Lower Egypt on the Tanitic branch of the Nile, mentioned as older than Hebron in Numbers 13:22. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html)

**Thebes (No)**: Keil explains the name as probably “abode of Amon” (Egyptian *P-amen*, “house of Amon”), the sacred name of Thebes, the celebrated royal city of Upper Egypt, the Διὸς πόλις ἡ μεγάλη of the Greeks. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html)

---

### v. 15 — “I will pour out My wrath on Pelusium, the stronghold of Egypt, and cut off the crowds of Thebes.”

**Pelusium (Sin)**: The name means “mire” (like Greek πηλός, “clay”). It stood on the eastern branch of the Nile surrounded by swamps, and its position made it “the key of Egypt.” Suidas describes it as “the key both of the entrance and exit of Egypt.” Strabo notes: “Egypt is difficult of access here from places in the East.” The Pulpit Commentary says Ezekiel, in calling it “the strength of Egypt,” must have known its local characteristics. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html)

---

### v. 16 — “I will set fire to Egypt, Pelusium will writhe in anguish, Thebes will be split open, and Memphis will face daily distress.”

The Pulpit Commentary notes the phrase “distresses daily” (KJV; BSB “daily distress”): Hitzig and Keil take it as “troubles in the day-time” — the city would be attacked in open day, not by night (cf. “the spoiler at noonday,” Jeremiah 15:8). Keil says: “The enemy who comes by day … is the enemy who does not shun open attack.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html)

---

### v. 17 — “The young men of On and Pi-beseth will fall by the sword, and those cities will go into captivity.”

**On (Aven)**: Heliopolis, the “house of the sun” (Jeremiah 43:13), one of the principal seats of Egyptian sun-worship, with a celebrated temple and learned priesthood. The form *Aven* (Hebrew for “a vain thing” or “idol,” as in Hosea 4:15; 10:5) “was perhaps chosen as a word of scorn pointing to the idolatry of the city.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html)

**Pi-beseth**: Bubastos/Bubastis, named after the cat-headed goddess Pasht (the Egyptian Diana). It lay on the royal canal leading to Suez. Destroyed by the Persians, only heaps of ruins remain today at Tel Bastah. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html)

**“Those cities will go into captivity”**: Keil notes the feminine pronoun *hennah* refers to the cities themselves — their civil population as distinguished from the military garrison (“young men”). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html)

---

### v. 18 — “The day will be darkened in Tahpanhes when I break the yoke of Egypt … A cloud will cover her, and her daughters will go into captivity.”

**Tahpanhes** (Tehaphnehes): The Daphne of Herodotus, a frontier fortress near Pelusium, built by Psammetichus, with a royal palace (Jeremiah 43:9). After Jerusalem’s fall, a remnant of Jews fled there, and Jeremiah predicted God’s judgment upon them there (Jeremiah 43–44). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html)

**“The day shall be darkened”**: The normal prophetic image for the departure of the sunshine of prosperity (cf. Amos 5:20; 8:9; Isaiah 5:30; Jeremiah 13:16). Keil says the darkening of the day is “the phenomenal prognostic of the dawning of the great day of judgment upon the nations (cf. Joel 2:10; 3:4, 15; Isaiah 13:10).” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-30.html)

**“Break the yoke of Egypt”**: The Pulpit Commentary notes an interpretive difficulty — elsewhere “breaking the yoke” means deliverance from oppression, but here it clearly means God breaking the yoke of power with which Egypt had subjugated other nations. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html)

**“Her daughters”**: Either the literal women who would be taken captive (as the “young men” fell by the sword, v. 17), or figuratively the dependent towns and villages. The Pulpit Commentary favours the literal meaning, given the mention of “young men” in the previous verse. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html)

---

### v. 19 — “So I will execute judgment on Egypt, and they will know that I am the LORD.”

The summary statement closing the first oracle. Guzik notes: “God would reveal Himself through His judgments. Every observant eye could and would see that the God of Israel, Yahweh (the LORD), was Lord and God.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/)

---

### v. 20 — “In the eleventh year, on the seventh day of the first month, the word of the LORD came to me…”

This is April 586 BC, about three and a half months before the fall of Jerusalem. The Pulpit Commentary notes this was written “at or about the time of the abortive attempt of Pharaoh-Hophra to come to the relief of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 34:21; 37:5–7).” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html) Ellicott confirms: “Very likely this prophecy had its occasion in the temporary raising of the siege of Jerusalem by Pharaoh-Hophra, and Nebuchadnezzar’s driving him away.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-30.html)

Guzik adds the context: “Many were still looking to Egypt in hope of help from her … God wanted Jerusalem and Judah to know that Egypt had no power, no strength to help her” (quoting Morgan). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/)

---

### v. 21 — “Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt. See, it has not been bound up for healing, or splinted for strength to hold the sword.”

**The broken arm**: The Pulpit Commentary says the metaphor was familiar (Ezekiel 17:9; 22:6; 1 Samuel 2:31; Jeremiah 48:25), but Ezekiel’s characteristic method is to follow the figure into surgical detail — “A man with a broken arm might be cured and fight again; but it was not to be so with Pharaoh. His arm was not to be bound with a roller … The Hebrew word for ‘roller’ is not found elsewhere, and Ezekiel’s use of it is one of the instances of his knowledge of surgery.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html)

**Egyptian cultural background**: Guzik (quoting Alexander) notes that “the flexed arm was a common Egyptian symbol for the Pharaoh’s strength. Often statues or images of the Pharaoh have this arm flexed, wielding a sword in battle. A king with great biceps was especially a popular concept under the Saites Dynasty of Ezekiel’s day. In addition Hophra took a second formal title that meant ‘possessed of a muscular arm’ or ‘strong-armed.’” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/)

**Historical referent**: Ellicott says the perfect tense “I have broken” refers to the breaking of Egypt’s power by former Assyrian conquests, “and perhaps especially to the great battle of Carchemish (about twenty years before), in which Egypt received a blow from which she never recovered.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-30.html) The Pulpit Commentary identifies it more specifically with Hophra’s failed attempt to relieve Jerusalem (Jeremiah 37:5–7). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html)

---

### v. 22 — “Therefore … I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt. I will break his arms, both the strong one and the one already broken…”

**“The strong, and that which was broken”**: Ellicott explains this means “the whole power of Egypt, both in so far as already crippled, and in so far as it still retained strength.” A warrior whose sword-arm was broken might fight with his left; God would break the left arm too — total incapacitation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-30.html)

The Pulpit Commentary: “The left arm also should be broken as the right had been. The Chaldean king should wax stronger and stronger.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html)

---

### v. 23 — “I will disperse the Egyptians among the nations and scatter them throughout the lands.”

Repeated verbatim from Ezekiel 29:12 and again in v. 26. The Pulpit Commentary calls it “the dispersion which was the almost inevitable sequel of an Oriental conquest.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html)

---

### v. 24 — “I will strengthen the arms of Babylon’s king and place My sword in his hand, but I will break the arms of Pharaoh, who will groan before him like a mortally wounded man.”

**Contrast of strength**: God strengthens Nebuchadnezzar while breaking Pharaoh. Guzik: “Even as God weakened Egypt and made Pharaoh defenseless, God would also strengthen Nebuchadnezzar and even give him the sword of God’s judgment.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/)

**“My sword in his hand”**: The Pulpit Commentary says: “The sword of Nebuchadnezzar should be as truly ‘the sword of Jehovah,’ as that of Gideon had been (Judges 7:18).” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html)

**“Groan … like a mortally wounded man”**: Guzik quotes Block: “The prediction that he will groan [lit. ‘groan groanings’] before him like one slain implies that Pharaoh himself will be killed.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/) Guzik also notes that “by the time Nebuchadrezzar invaded Egypt, after the siege of Tyre was ended, Hophra had been killed in civil war … by a rival faction under Ahmose” (quoting Taylor). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/)

Guzik adds the theological point: “These apparently mighty monarchs of Egypt and Babylon were both in the hands of Jehovah. Their apparent successes and failures resulted from His action. They were completely in His power” (quoting Morgan). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/)

---

### v. 25 — “I will strengthen the arms of Babylon’s king, but Pharaoh’s arms will fall limp. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I place My sword in the hand of Babylon’s king…”

**“My sword”**: F. B. Meyer (cited at preceptaustin.org) emphasises the word “my”: “The punishment inflicted by the king of Babylon on Egypt was directly from God; it was his sword in the hand of Nebuchadnezzar … How little the historian of that time realized that there was anything more in the expedition of Babylon against Egypt than the natural rivalry of these two great nations. But the eye of the inspired seer saw that Babylon was the executor of the Divine decree.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel-f_b_meyer)

---

### v. 26 — “I will disperse the Egyptians among the nations and scatter them throughout the lands. Then they will know that I am the LORD.”

Gill summarises the theological purpose: “whose name alone is Jehovah, and does whatsoever he pleases; sets up kings, and puts them down; strengthens and weakens kingdoms just as seems good in his sight; none having any power but what is given by him, and which he can take away when he thinks fit.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/30.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary concludes: “There in the land of exile they should see that they had been fighting against God; and so the prophet ends the chapter with his ever-recurring formula, They shall know that I am Jehovah.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html)

---

## Theological Distinctives and Traditions

For this chapter, the traditional Protestant commentaries surveyed (Gill – Baptist-leaning; Guzik/Enduring Word – charismatic/Pentecostal; Pulpit, Keil & Delitzsch, Ellicott – broadly Protestant/Reformed heritage) show **substantial agreement** on the plain meaning. No major doctrinal flashpoints emerge from this judgment oracle. The following points can be noted:

- **Day of the LORD**: All traditions read this as a local, historical day of judgment on Egypt, while also seeing it as a pattern of the final eschatological Day of the Lord. Guzik (charismatic) quotes J. B. Wright: “From time to time a nation reaches a climax … The final Day is yet to come … Thus previous Days of the Lord become patterns of the final Day.” The Pulpit Commentary (broadly Protestant) says the same. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-30/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html)

- **“Covenant land” (v. 5)**: Some older interpreters (Jerome, the LXX translators, and some Catholic tradition) read this as a reference to Jews in Egypt — “the children of my covenant.” The Pulpit Commentary and Keil discuss this view but lean toward an unknown allied people. This is a text-critical and interpretive question, not a sharp denominational divide. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-30.html; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/30.htm)

- **God’s sovereignty over nations**: The Reformed emphasis on God’s absolute sovereignty over all nations — using even pagan Babylon as His instrument — is prominent across all the commentaries. Gill (Baptist) and Keil (Lutheran/Reformed) are in full agreement that both Nebuchadnezzar and Pharaoh were entirely in God’s hands.
